Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette:
At eighty years old, Eleanor Vance had believed she understood the architecture of a good life, one built on a foundation of predictable kindness and mutual respect. A long career as a social worker had fortified this belief; she had seen the worst of things, but always held that systems, and people, could ultimately be trusted. Meeting Arthur two years ago had felt like a capstone to that life, a partnership for her final decades. That foundation crumbled six months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. The memory doesn’t play like a film for her. Instead, it is a series of stark, silent photographs burned into her mind: the heavy oak of their apartment door slamming shut with a deafening crack, the contorted anger on Arthur’s face under the hallway light, the pattern of the floral wallpaper in the corner she was backed into. She cannot string these moments together into a coherent sequence, but the images float up, untethered from time, bringing with them a wave of grief so profound it feels like drowning.

In the weeks that followed, Eleanor’s world began to shrink. The first thing to go was sleep. She would lie awake for hours, heart pounding, listening to the old building settle, certain that every creak was a footstep. She started staying up until two or three in the morning, reading in her armchair until sheer exhaustion took over, a desperate strategy to avoid the nightmares that waited for her in the dark. During the day, a relentless watchfulness took hold. When her nephew, Mark, came to visit, she couldn't relax. She found herself tracking his every move, her body tensed for a threat she couldn't name but felt in her bones. The sound of the elevator door opening on her floor would send a jolt of adrenaline through her. After she cancelled their weekly dinner for the third time, Mark stopped asking. She felt the loss of his company keenly, but the thought of being alone with any man, even one she had helped raise, was simply unbearable.

Her professional instincts turned inward, twisting into a painful, circular logic. She spends hours trying to understand *why* it happened, replaying conversations, searching for a missed sign, a misstep on her part that could have prevented it. This quest for meaning provides no answers, only a deepening conviction that the world she knew was a fiction. Her core belief system, once a source of strength, has been completely destroyed. People, she has come to believe, cannot be trusted. Safety is an illusion. This new reality dictates her every action. Before entering the local library or the grocery store, she pauses on the threshold, her eyes darting from one exit to another, mapping escape routes before she dares to step inside.

Eleanor feels a profound sense of being soiled, contaminated by the event. She showers twice a day, scrubbing her skin raw, but the feeling of being unclean lingers. She tries to consciously push the memory away, to will the photographic snapshots out of her mind, but they always return, vivid and sharp. It was the growing isolation that finally prompted her to seek help. The silence in her apartment had become as loud as the slamming door in her memory. She is terrified that she is permanently broken, that the trust and openness that defined her for eight decades are gone for good. More than anything, she hopes to one day feel safe in her own home again, to be able to hear a door close without her body preparing for an attack that is already over.
